etymology: From the Saxon forheafod, “fore-head,” the front of the head above the eyes; rendering the Hebrew metsach, the brow, and the Greek metopon, that part of the face which cannot be hidden and which therefore carries whatever mark is set upon it.
biblical_def: The forehead in Scripture is the open face of a man — the one part of him that goes before him into every room and can conceal nothing. Because it cannot be hidden, it becomes the appointed place of allegiance. Upon the high priest’s brow was bound the golden plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD, “always upon his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD” (Exo 28:38): the mediator wears the acceptance of the people where all may read it. When Ezekiel is sent to a rebellious house, the LORD hardens the prophet’s brow to match theirs — “As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead” (Eze 3:9) — not a stubborn heart, but a face that will not blush before scoffers. Set against this is Judah’s “whore’s forehead” (Jer 3:3), brazenness that has lost the very power of shame. And in judgment the brow is where God distinguishes His own: the mark set upon the men that sigh and cry for the abominations of the city (Eze 9:4), and the sealing of the servants of God in their foreheads before the winds are loosed (Rev 7:3). Satan can only counterfeit; the mark in the right hand or in the forehead (Rev 13:16) is the devil’s parody of a seal he cannot make. Two brows, two owners, and no third party: every man is publicly marked, and the mark is read by God before it is read by men.
webster_summary: The front of the head above the eyes; hence the open, unhidden part of a man, and in Scripture the appointed place of a mark, a plate, or a seal declaring whose he is.
webster_full: FOREHEAD, n. The part of the face which extends from the hair on the top of the head to the eyes.
From fore and head; Saxon forheafod.
Impudence; audaciousness; assurance; as in a brazen or a whore’s forehead (Jer 3:3).
The place appointed for the high priest’s golden plate, engraven HOLINESS TO THE LORD (Exo 28:36–38).
In prophetic Scripture, the place of a distinguishing mark or seal (Eze 9:4; Rev 7:3; 13:16).
scriptures: Eze 3:9
As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house.
Eze 9:4

And the LORD said unto him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof.

And it shall be upon Aaron's forehead, that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow in all their holy gifts; and it shall be always upon his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD.
Rev 7:3
Saying, Hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees, till we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads.
corruption_summary: Rev 13:16’s mark in the forehead has been turned into a barcode-and-microchip spectacle by dispensational date-setting, which reads a sign of open allegiance as a technology and sells the reading in paperbacks.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is sensationalism. Since Darby and Scofield in the nineteenth century, and industrially since the 1970s, dispensational premillennialism has taught readers to hunt the mark of the beast among credit cards, national identity numbers, implanted chips, and whatever technology is newest at the printing of the book. Every generation of that literature has named its candidate, every generation’s candidate has aged into embarrassment, and the church has been trained to read Revelation as a puzzle about hardware rather than a comfort about the Lamb. The dictionary rejects dispensational premillennialism outright as a novelty absent from every Reformation confession, and rejects its handling of this text in particular. Note what the sensational reading destroys: it severs Rev 13:16 from Rev 7:3, which it plainly answers. The sealing of the servants of God in their foreheads comes first; the mark in the right hand or in the forehead is the imitation. Satan is not an inventor, he is a forger, and a forgery is only intelligible next to the genuine article — the priestly plate on Aaron’s brow, the ink-mark of Eze 9:4, the seal of the Spirit on the believer.

Recover the plain sense: the forehead is where allegiance is public. The hand is what a man does and the forehead is what a man openly is, and Scripture marks both because a man serves with his labour and confesses with his face. To be sealed in the forehead is to belong to God visibly and irrevocably, and no one who reads Eze 9:4 will think the mark is placed on the indifferent: it is set on the men that sigh and that cry over the abominations of the city, that is, upon the grieving remnant. Two practical consequences follow. First, the believer’s comfort in an evil day is not that he will outwit a numbering system but that he is already sealed. Second, the believer’s duty is Ezekiel’s — a brow made adamant, a face that will not colour before a rebellious house. Brazenness that cannot blush (Jer 3:3) and boldness that will not flinch look alike to the world and are opposites before God; the difference is entirely whose name is written on the brow.
roots_summary: The unhidden front of the head; hence the appointed place of a plate, a mark, or a seal, declaring openly whose a man is.
roots_lines: Forehead — Saxon forheafod, the fore part of the head.
Hebrew metsach, the brow (Exo 28:38; Eze 3:9; Jer 3:3).
Greek metopon, literally “between the eyes” (Rev 7:3; 13:16).
Because it cannot be hidden, it is the biblical site of open allegiance.
The mark of Rev 13:16 is the counterfeit of the seal of Rev 7:3, not its original.
usage: The high priest bore acceptance on his brow (Exo 28:38) — Christ bears ours where all may read it.
Ezekiel’s adamant forehead is courage, not obstinacy; Jeremiah’s whore’s forehead is shamelessness.
Read the mark of Rev 13:16 backwards from Rev 7:3: forgery presupposes an original seal.

etymology: From the Saxon thuma, the short thick finger set opposite the rest; rendering the Hebrew bohen yad, literally the thumb of the hand, the member without which the hand can grasp nothing.
biblical_def: The thumb is the member that makes a hand a hand: without it the fingers close on nothing. Scripture gives it a fixed and remarkable place in the ritual of consecration. At the ordaining of Aaron and his sons the blood of the ram was put “upon the tip of the right ear… and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot” (Exo 29:20), and Moses did precisely so at the altar (Lev 8:24). The identical rite is performed over the cleansed leper, blood and then oil upon ear, thumb, and toe (Lev 14:14), so that a man restored to the camp is consecrated by the same three touches that ordain a priest. The three members are not chosen at random. The ear is what he hears, the thumb is what he does, the great toe is where he walks; blood upon them claims hearing, working, and walking — the whole man, and the right side of him, his readiest strength. Nothing is left to the man’s own disposal. The dark inversion of the figure stands in Judges: the seventy kings whose thumbs and great toes Adoni-bezek had cut off, gathering meat under his table, until his own thumbs and toes were taken and he confessed, “as I have done, so God hath requited me” (Jdg 1:6–7). To take a man’s thumbs is to unmake his labour; to bloody a man’s thumb at the altar is to claim it.
webster_summary: The short thick finger of the hand, set opposite the others; in the Levitical rites one of the three members — ear, thumb, and great toe — touched with blood in consecration and cleansing.
webster_full: THUMB, n. The short thick finger of the human hand, or the corresponding member of an animal.
Saxon thuma; allied to the Latin pollex, the finger of strength.
It is set opposite the other fingers, and by it the hand grasps and holds; hence a figure for capacity to labour.
Hebrew bohen, used of both the thumb of the hand and the great toe of the foot.
Anointed with blood at the consecration of priests (Exo 29:20; Lev 8:24) and at the cleansing of the leper (Lev 14:14).
scriptures: Then shalt thou kill the ram, and take of his blood, and put it upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron, and upon the tip of the right ear of his sons, and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot, and sprinkle the blood upon the altar round about.
Lev 8:24

And he brought Aaron's sons, and Moses put of the blood upon the tip of their right ear, and upon the thumbs of their right hands, and upon the great toes of their right feet: and Moses sprinkled the blood upon the altar round about.

And the priest shall take some of the blood of the trespass offering, and the priest shall put it upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot:
Jdg 1:6
But Adonibezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes.
corruption_summary: The live misuse is partial consecration — a religion of the ear that never reaches the thumb, hearing much and doing little, as though God claimed a compartment of a man rather than the whole of him.
corruption_paragraphs: The abiding temptation the thumb exposes is a consecration that stops at the ear. Blood was put on three members, not one, and the order is instructive: hearing first, because faith comes by hearing, then the working hand and the walking foot, because a hearing that never reaches the hand is what James calls deceiving one’s own self. Modern religious life has a settled habit of dividing a man into a sacred compartment and a secular one — sermons, songs, and devotions on the one side; trade, labour, money, and the ordinary week on the other — and of supposing God has claimed the first and left the second to the man’s own discretion. The Levitical rite forbids that division at the outset. It is the right thumb, the strong working member of the strong hand, that is bloodied at the altar; a man’s craft, his contract, his tools, and his wages are consecrated ground. The same three touches are laid on the cleansed leper, which is to say that the man brought back from exclusion is not merely permitted to rejoin the camp but claimed for service in it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that redemption claims the entire man, body and soul, and claims him by blood. “Ye are not your own… for ye are bought with a price” (1Co 6:19–20) is the New Testament of the ear, thumb, and toe. Christ our great High Priest was consecrated to a work that used every member — ears open to the Father’s will, hands that healed and were pierced, feet that went about doing good and were nailed — and He gives His people the same undivided consecration. So the believer yields his members as instruments of righteousness unto God (Rom 6:13), which is a whole-body doctrine, not a sentiment. Adoni-bezek stands at the other pole as a warning of exact retribution: he unmade seventy men’s hands and lost his own, and he knew the ledger was God’s. The thumb that God claims at the altar, God may also require at the judgment.
roots_summary: The grasping member of the hand; with ear and great toe, one of the three parts touched with blood to consecrate the whole man.
roots_lines: Thumb — Saxon thuma, the thick finger by which the hand grasps.
Hebrew bohen, used alike of the thumb and the great toe.
Ear, thumb, toe: what a man hears, what he does, where he walks.
The right side is specified — the readiest strength is claimed first.
The same rite ordains a priest (Exo 29:20) and restores a leper (Lev 14:14).
usage: Blood on the thumb consecrates a man’s labour, not merely his devotions.
The leper is cleansed by the priest’s own ordination rite — restored and claimed in one act.
Adoni-bezek’s severed thumbs are exact requital; he confessed the justice himself.

etymology: From the Saxon nafela, the centre or nave of the belly; rendering the Hebrew shor and shorer, the navel or umbilical cord, the mark left in the flesh where a child was once wholly sustained by another.
biblical_def: The navel is the scar of dependence. Every man carries in his own body the plain evidence that he did not make himself, was not self-sustaining, and once received all he had through a cord he did not tie and could not cut. Scripture uses it in exactly that sober register. To the son who keeps wisdom and departs from evil the promise is bodily: “It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones” (Pro 3:8) — the fear of the LORD reaching the frame itself, from the centre outward. Ezekiel draws the harder picture. Israel’s origin was a newborn cast out in the open field: “in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all” (Eze 16:4) — no midwife, no covering, no claim on anyone. And into that helplessness the LORD comes: “when thou wast in thy blood, Live” (Eze 16:6). The covenant does not find a nation attractive; it finds an unwashed infant and speaks life over it. That is unmerited love with the sentiment taken out. The Song can praise the beloved’s body without shame (Son 7:2), because the body is God’s handiwork and the marriage bed is undefiled. The navel therefore says two things at once: you were made, and you were kept, and neither was your doing.
webster_summary: The centre of the lower part of the belly, where the umbilical cord was attached; the bodily mark of a creature’s origin and utter early dependence.
webster_full: NAVEL, n. The centre of the lower part of the abdomen; the point where the umbilical cord of the foetus was attached.
Saxon nafela, from nafa, the nave or centre of a wheel.
Hence figuratively, the middle or central part of any thing.
Hebrew shor, the navel; shorer, the navel-string or cord (Pro 3:8; Eze 16:4).
Used in Scripture of bodily health (Pro 3:8) and of the helplessness of the newborn (Eze 16:4).
scriptures: Pro 3:8
It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones.
Eze 16:4
And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all.
Eze 16:6
And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live; yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live.
Son 7:2
Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies.
corruption_summary: Modernity has revived the old gnostic severing of the self from the body — the transgender claim that a man’s embodied sex is incidental to who he really is — against Gen 1:27, Psa 139, and 1Co 6:19–20.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is ancient wearing new dress. The second-century gnostics taught that the true self is a spark imprisoned in matter and that the body is at best a container and at worst a mistake; the church answered them with the doctrines of creation, incarnation, and bodily resurrection, and the answer has never needed revision. The present form of the error is the claim that a person has a “gender identity” distinct from and authoritative over his body, so that the flesh he was born in may be overruled, medicated, and cut to match an inward sense of self — the very categories “gender assigned at birth” and “gender identity” being the corruption, not merely their misuse. Scripture forecloses it at the first chapter: “male and female created he them” (Gen 1:27), which our Lord treats as settled and sufficient (Mat 19:4). Sex is creational, embodied, and immutable; it is not a costume the self wears, nor a construct the will assigns. The navel is a quiet witness against the whole scheme, for it is the mark of a body received rather than chosen — you were knit together in a womb (Psa 139:13–14), fed by a cord, and delivered into a world you did not consult.

Recover the doctrine that the body is the man, not the man’s property. “Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body” (1Co 6:19–20). The believer’s flesh is bought, indwelt, and destined for resurrection; it is not raw material. And with the doctrine, recover the pastoral use of Eze 16. The image is deliberately unsparing: an infant in her blood, cord uncut, unwashed, unsalted, unswaddled, exposed in an open field. That is what God’s love found, and He did not find it lovely. He spoke — Live — and it lived. Every soul that is in Christ owes its whole existence to a word spoken over it while it was still repulsive, which is why boasting is excluded and why compassion toward image-bearers caught in this present confusion is a duty, not a concession. Tell them the truth about the body precisely because the body will be raised.
roots_summary: The centre of the belly where the cord was attached; the body’s own record that life was received, not generated.
roots_lines: Navel — Saxon nafela, from nafa, the nave or hub of a wheel; hence a centre.
Hebrew shor (navel) and shorer (navel-string, Eze 16:4).
Pro 3:8 makes the fear of the LORD bodily health, from the centre outward.
Eze 16:4 is the covenant’s origin story: an infant with the cord uncut.
The mark is universal; no man carries it by his own arrangement.
usage: Pro 3:8 promises health to the navel — wisdom reaches the frame, not only the mind.
Eze 16:4 is unmerited love with the sentiment removed: God’s love found nothing lovely.
The navel answers every claim that the self stands free of the body it was born in.

etymology: From jaw, of uncertain Northern origin, with bone; rendering the Hebrew lechi, the jaw or cheek, which also gave its name to the place Lehi where Samson fought, and to Ramath-lehi, the lifting up of the jawbone.
biblical_def: The jawbone enters Scripture as the least likely weapon ever carried into a battle. Bound with new cords and delivered to the Philistines at Lehi, Samson felt the Spirit of the LORD come mightily upon him, and the cords became as burnt flax (Jdg 15:14); then “he found a new jawbone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith” (Jdg 15:15). Every particular of the instrument is a disqualification. It is bone, not iron, in an age when Israel had no smith; it is the jaw of an ass, the unclean beast of burden; and it is found lying on the ground, neither forged nor bought nor chosen. Against it stood a nation with chariots. The point is not Samson’s strength, which was never his own — the text says plainly that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him first — but God’s settled way of working. He saves by ram’s horns and clay pitchers, by a sling and a stone, by five loaves, by the foolishness of preaching: “God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27). Samson afterward named the place Ramath-lehi and, dying of thirst in his victory, called on the LORD and was given water — lest the man who had just killed a thousand should imagine the arm was his. The jawbone is a sermon on means: God’s power is glorified in instruments that can claim nothing.
webster_summary: The bone of the jaw, in which the teeth are fixed; famously the weapon Samson found at Lehi and with which he slew a thousand Philistines.
webster_full: JAWBONE, n. The bone of either jaw, in which the teeth are fixed.
From jaw and bone; the Hebrew word lechi denotes the jaw or the cheek.
The same word names the place Lehi, and Ramath-lehi, the lifting up of the jawbone (Jdg 15:17).
The weapon with which Samson slew a thousand men (Jdg 15:15–16).
Hence proverbially, an instrument of no account made mighty by the hand that wields it.
scriptures: And when he came unto Lehi, the Philistines shouted against him: and the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the cords that were upon his arms became as flax that was burnt with fire, and his bands loosed from off his hands.
And he found a new jawbone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: The common misuse turns Samson into a strongman and the jawbone into a trophy of personal grit, when the text puts the Spirit of the LORD before the weapon and thirst after the victory.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is heroic moralism. Samson is preached as a study in wasted potential or, worse, as an emblem of raw masculine force, and the jawbone becomes a symbol of what a determined man can do with whatever is at hand — a proverb for self-reliance. The narrative resists that reading at every turn. The Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him before he touched the bone (Jdg 15:14); the weapon was found, not made; the man who had slain a thousand collapsed within the hour, so athirst that he thought he would die and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised, and had to beg water of the God he had just been used by. Samson is not the point of Samson. He is a judge raised, gifted, indulged, and finally broken, whose deliverances are God’s and whose sins are his own, and the Spirit-given strength never once became a possession he could manage. Read as self-help, the chapter flatters the reader; read as it stands, it humbles him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God chooses unlikely means so that the glory cannot be reassigned. “God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27), and Paul learned the same lesson in his own flesh: strength made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9). The pattern runs the length of Scripture — a shepherd’s sling against a giant, trumpets against a walled city, a boy’s loaves against a hungry multitude, and at the centre a crucified Man against the powers of darkness, which is the greatest apparent weakness and the actual conquest. The comfort for the ordinary believer is direct: God is not waiting for you to become a suitable instrument. The jawbone of an ass was not upgraded before it was used. What He requires is a hand that will pick it up when He says so, and a mouth that will ask Him for water afterward instead of composing a song about its own arm.
roots_summary: The bone of the jaw; the found, unclean, unlikely weapon by which God delivered Israel through Samson at Lehi.
roots_lines: Jawbone — jaw + bone; Hebrew lechi, jaw or cheek.
Lehi the place and lechi the jaw are the same word (Jdg 15:9, 15).
Ramath-lehi = the lifting up (or casting away) of the jawbone (Jdg 15:17).
The bone of an ass is unclean, brittle, and found — every disqualification at once.
The Spirit precedes the weapon in the text; the order is the doctrine.
usage: Jdg 15:14 comes before Jdg 15:15: the Spirit first, the jawbone second.
God’s instruments are chosen for their unfitness, that no flesh should glory.
Samson begging water an hour after slaying a thousand is the safeguard against hero-worship.

etymology: From fore and skin, rendering the Hebrew orlah, the uncircumcised part; used literally of the flesh cut away in the covenant sign, and figuratively of the uncircumcised heart, ear, and lip.
biblical_def: The foreskin is the flesh removed in the sign God gave to Abraham: “ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you” (Gen 17:11). Scripture speaks of it plainly, and so must a dictionary. The sign was cut in the body, in the male, at eight days, in the seat of generation — that is, upon the very fountain of the seed, marking that the promised Seed and the whole line He would come through belonged to the LORD. It was blood, and it was permanent, and it was borne in the flesh where no man could display it for praise. Yet from the beginning the sign pointed past itself. Moses commands the thing signified in the same words: circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked; and he promises what no knife can accomplish — “the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart… to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart” (Deu 30:6). Paul draws the line where Moses drew it: “circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God” (Rom 2:29). And in Christ the outward rite is fulfilled and finished: believers are “circumcised with the circumcision made without hands… by the circumcision of Christ” (Col 2:11), a cutting away of the body of the sins of the flesh accomplished at the cross and applied by the Spirit in regeneration.
webster_summary: The fold of skin removed in circumcision; in Scripture the flesh cut away as the token of the Abrahamic covenant, and figuratively the uncircumcision of the heart.
webster_full: FORESKIN, n. The prepuce; a prolongation of the cutis of the penis, covering the glans.
From fore and skin; Hebrew orlah, that which is uncircumcised.
The part removed in circumcision, appointed as the token of the covenant with Abraham (Gen 17:11).
Used figuratively of the heart (Deu 10:16), the ear (Jer 6:10), and the lips (Exo 6:12), for what is closed and unyielding toward God.
In the New Testament the outward rite is fulfilled in the circumcision made without hands (Col 2:11).
scriptures: And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
Deu 30:6
And the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live.
Jer 4:4

Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: lest my fury come forth like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.
Col 2:11
In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ:
corruption_summary: The oldest corruption is the sign trusted in place of the thing signified — a cut foreskin and an uncut heart — which is precisely the error Moses, the prophets, and Paul all attack.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Scripture itself names is the confidence of the flesh: a man bearing the covenant token in his body and having no covenant in his heart. Israel fell into it constantly, which is why Moses, Jeremiah, and Paul all reach for the same figure — uncircumcised hearts, uncircumcised ears, uncircumcised lips — to say that the outward mark saves nobody. Paul’s verdict is blunt: he is not a Jew which is one outwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart (Rom 2:28–29). The modern form of the same error is not confined to any one ordinance; wherever a sign is treated as though it conveyed the grace it signifies, a man is being taught to rest on a rite. A second and lesser modern flattening deserves mention: the reduction of Gen 17 to an ancient hygienic custom or a tribal boundary-marker, as though the LORD had merely regularised a practice. He did not. He said token of the covenant, and He attached a curse to neglect of it.

There is a genuine in-house disagreement about what succeeds circumcision under the new covenant, and it should be stated honestly rather than blurred. Reformed paedobaptists argue from the continuity of the covenant of grace that the children of believers are to receive the initiatory sign as Abraham’s children did, and the Westminster Confession stands in that line and is honoured here as the great Reformed-Presbyterian parallel. The dictionary, holding the 1689 London Baptist Confession, teaches believer’s baptism: Col 2:11–12 joins circumcision-made-without-hands to burial and rising with Christ “through the faith of the operation of God,” so that the new covenant sign follows the profession of faith it signifies, and the new covenant community is constituted of those who all know the LORD (Jer 31:34; Heb 8:11). Both sides confess the same gospel and the same imputed righteousness; they differ on the subjects of the sign. What neither may do is repeat Israel’s mistake in a new dress — substituting an administered rite for the circumcision of the heart, which God alone performs and which alone makes a man love Him (Deu 30:6).
roots_summary: The flesh cut away in the covenant sign given to Abraham; from the first a figure of the heart that God alone can circumcise.
roots_lines: Foreskin — fore + skin; Hebrew orlah, the uncircumcised part.
Gen 17:11 makes the cut flesh a token — a sign of a covenant, not the covenant itself.
The sign was set in the seat of generation, marking the promised Seed’s line as the LORD’s.
Moses already applies the figure inwardly: the foreskin of the heart (Deu 10:16; 30:6).
Col 2:11 names the fulfilment: circumcision made without hands, by the circumcision of Christ.
usage: The token was borne where no man could display it — a sign for God to read, not an ornament.
Rom 2:29 is Moses’ own doctrine, not a Pauline innovation: the heart, not the letter.
Circumcision of the heart is God’s work (Deu 30:6); no knife and no rite can imitate it.

etymology: From eye and the Saxon hlid, a cover or lid; rendering the Hebrew aphappayim, a dual form from a root meaning to flutter or flash, hence the covers that open and close upon the eye.
biblical_def: The eyelids are the covers that open and close upon the eye, and Scripture uses them for three things: God’s examining gaze, a man’s fixed attention, and the wakefulness of grief or resolve. The first is the weightiest. “The LORD is in his holy temple, the LORD’S throne is in heaven: his eyes behold, his eyelids try, the children of men” (Psa 11:4). The figure is of a narrowing gaze — the lids drawn close as a man squints to examine a thing minutely. God does not merely see; He inspects, weighs, and assays. That is set in a psalm written while the wicked bend their bow in the dark, and it is the answer to it: the throne is not vacant and the examination is already under way. The second use is direction. “Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee” (Pro 4:25) — the wise man’s gaze is governed, not wandering, because what the eye lingers on the heart soon follows. The third is the eyelid that will not close: David swearing he will not give slumber to his eyelids until he find a place for the LORD (Psa 132:4), and Jeremiah’s mourning women whose eyelids gush out with waters (Jer 9:18). Zeal and lamentation both keep the lids open; indifference sleeps.
webster_summary: The covers of the eye, which open and close upon it; in Scripture a figure of God’s minute examination of men, of governed attention, and of sleepless zeal or grief.
webster_full: EYELID, n. The cover of the eye; that portion of movable skin with which an animal covers or uncovers the eyeball at pleasure.
From eye and Saxon hlid, a lid or cover.
Hebrew aphappayim, a dual noun, from a root signifying to flutter or flash.
Ascribed to God by figure: his eyelids try the children of men (Psa 11:4), as one narrows the eyes to examine closely.
Used of sleeplessness from zeal (Psa 132:4) or from weeping (Jer 9:18).
scriptures: Psa 11:4
The LORD is in his holy temple, the LORD'S throne is in heaven: his eyes behold, his eyelids try, the children of men.
Pro 4:25
Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee.
I will not give sleep to mine eyes, or slumber to mine eyelids,
Jer 9:18
And let them make haste, and take up a wailing for us, that our eyes may run down with tears, and our eyelids gush out with waters.
corruption_summary: The examining gaze of Psa 11:4 has been replaced in popular religion by a benignly approving one — a God who beholds but never tries, watches but never assays.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the quiet deletion of God’s scrutiny. Modern religious speech is full of the divine gaze in its comfortable half: God sees you, God is with you, God is watching over you. The other half of Psa 11:4 has been dropped. His eyelids try the children of men — the word is the assayer’s, used of metal put to the fire to prove what is base in it. A God who beholds without trying is a spectator; the God of Scripture is a Judge whose examination is continuous and exact, who tries the righteous as well as the wicked, and who is not deceived by the arrangement of a life for public view. Strip the trying out of the beholding and two things collapse at once. Assurance becomes sentiment, because it rests on God being agreeable rather than on Christ having satisfied. And holiness loses its motive, because a man behaves as if the audit will never come. The psalm makes the opposite use: it is precisely because the LORD is enthroned and examining that the righteous need not flee to the mountain when the foundations are destroyed.

Recover both halves and the doctrine of providence stands whole. The eyes that behold are the eyes that keep — He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep — and the eyelids that try are the eyelids of one who will judge the world in righteousness. For the believer these are the same comfort, because the trial has already been met in Christ, whose righteousness the Father examines and approves on his behalf. Then follow the practical use in Pro 4:25, which comes immediately after “keep thy heart with all diligence” (Pro 4:23) and belongs to it: the eyelids are to look straight before thee. What a man permits his eyes to rest upon he is training his heart to want, which is why Job made a covenant with his eyes and why the discipline of the gaze is not prudery but wisdom. And let the lids stay open where Scripture keeps them open — David’s refusal of sleep until a place was found for the LORD, and Jeremiah’s weeping over a city under judgment. Zeal and lamentation are the two wakefulnesses of a living faith.
roots_summary: The covers of the eye; used of God’s minute assaying of men, of governed attention, and of the sleeplessness of zeal and grief.
roots_lines: Eyelids — eye + Saxon hlid, a cover.
Hebrew aphappayim, dual, from a root meaning to flutter or flash.
Psa 11:4 — try is the assayer’s word: to prove metal, not merely to view it.
Pro 4:25 follows Pro 4:23: the governed gaze serves the guarded heart.
Open lids mark zeal (Psa 132:4) and mourning (Jer 9:18); sleep marks indifference.
usage: Psa 11:4 gives both halves: His eyes behold, and His eyelids try.
Pro 4:25 governs the gaze because the heart follows what the eye lingers on.
David would not give slumber to his eyelids until the LORD had a place — zeal keeps the lids open.

etymology: From the Saxon throte, the passage of the neck; rendering the Hebrew garon, the gullet or windpipe, and the Greek larugx, the larynx — the channel through which both breath and speech proceed.
biblical_def: The throat is the passage through which speech comes out of a man, and Scripture makes it the most damning exhibit in the case against him. David, describing his enemies, does not begin with their deeds: “there is no faithfulness in their mouth; their inward part is very wickedness; their throat is an open sepulchre; they flatter with their tongue” (Psa 5:9). The figure is deliberately foul. An open sepulchre is a grave with the stone rolled away, exhaling the stench of what lies rotting inside; so the throat, opened in speech, releases the corruption of the heart. Paul takes that verse up and sets it in the middle of his indictment of the whole race — Jew and Gentile, all under sin — where throat, tongue, lips, and mouth are arraigned in sequence (Rom 3:13). This is the doctrine of total depravity taken to the organ of speech: not that every man says the worst thing possible, but that the channel itself is defiled at the source, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh. The throat has a second and gentler use: it is what fails in prolonged prayer — “I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried” (Psa 69:3), a psalm the Gospels apply to Christ. And it is what a hard man seizes: the forgiven servant took his fellow by the throat over an hundred pence (Mat 18:28), the mercy he had received never reaching his hands.
webster_summary: The anterior part of the neck, and the passage through which breath and speech proceed; in Scripture a figure for the corruption of the heart made audible.
webster_full: THROAT, n. The anterior part of the neck of an animal, in which are the gullet and windpipe, or the passages for the food and breath.
Saxon throte; hence to throttle, to seize or stop the throat.
Hebrew garon, the gullet; Greek larugx, the larynx, the organ of the voice.
An open sepulchre: a figure for speech that exhales the corruption within (Psa 5:9; Rom 3:13).
To take by the throat, to seize violently, as the unmerciful servant did his fellow (Mat 18:28).
scriptures: Psa 5:9
For there is no faithfulness in their mouth; their inward part is very wickedness; their throat is an open sepulchre; they flatter with their tongue.
Rom 3:13
Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips:
Psa 69:3
I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.
But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest.
corruption_summary: Rom 3:13 is emptied wherever man is assumed basically good and speech-sin is relocated from the fallen heart to the hearer’s offence, so that words are judged by reception rather than by truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet at this word. The first is the denial of total depravity. Modern religion, evangelical as often as liberal, works from the premise that man is fundamentally decent and occasionally errs, so Rom 3:13 must be softened into a description of unusually bad men rather than an indictment of the race. Paul allows no such escape: he stacks the psalms deliberately — none righteous, none that understandeth, throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet — and concludes that every mouth may be stopped and all the world become guilty before God. The doctrine is not that men are as bad as they could be, but that no faculty came through the fall undefiled, the organ of speech least of all. The second corruption follows from the first: when depravity is denied, sins of speech are no longer measured against God’s law but against the offence taken by the hearer. Words become right or wrong according to who was hurt and how loudly, so that flattery and cowardice pass unrebuked while plain truth is treated as an injury. Scripture judges speech by its source and its truth, not by its reception.

Recover the sepulchre and the remedy together. The image is intended to disgust, because a man will not seek a Saviour for a habit he thinks is a manner of speaking. If the throat is an open grave, the problem is not vocabulary but a corpse, and no course in communication will cure it — only a new heart, out of whose abundance a new mouth speaks. That is exactly the order of Rom 3: the indictment ends at verse 20 so that the righteousness of God without the law may begin at verse 21. Then let the redeemed use the throat as Christ used it. Psa 69:3 shows a dried throat worn out with crying unto God, and that psalm is the Gospels’ own commentary on His passion; He wearied His voice in prayer for those whose voices were raised against Him. And let Mat 18:28 stand as the permanent warning: a man may have been forgiven ten thousand talents and still have hands at his brother’s throat. Forgiveness that never reaches the grip is not forgiveness received.
roots_summary: The passage of breath and speech; Scripture’s figure for the heart’s corruption made audible, and an open grave in the indictment of the race.
roots_lines: Throat — Saxon throte, the passage of the neck; whence throttle.
Hebrew garon, the gullet (Psa 5:9); Greek larugx, the voice-organ (Rom 3:13).
An open sepulchre — a grave unstopped, exhaling what rots within.
Paul quotes Psa 5:9 in the arraignment of the whole race (Rom 3:10–19).
A dried throat marks prolonged prayer (Psa 69:3); a seized throat marks unforgiveness (Mat 18:28).
usage: The throat is an open sepulchre — the corruption is in the heart, not merely the vocabulary.
Rom 3:13 indicts the race, not a class of unusually wicked men.
Psa 69:3’s dried throat belongs to the Man of sorrows praying for His enemies.

etymology: From the Old French joint, past participle of joindre, to join, from the Latin jungere; rendering the Hebrew qatar (the knitting of the loins) and the Greek harmos and haphe, the fittings and the contact-points by which the body holds together.
biblical_def: The joints are where the frame holds together, and Scripture uses them for three things: terror, division, and union. In terror, Belshazzar’s joints are loosed. The hand writes upon the plaister of the wall and “the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another” (Dan 5:6) — a man who could hold a kingdom cannot hold his own body upright when God writes his sentence. In division, the joints mark the finest possible seam: the word of God is quick and powerful, “piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” (Heb 4:12). No blade reaches so far. Scripture separates what a man cannot separate in himself, cutting between motive and motive, and it does so as a discerner, not merely as a description. In union, the joints are the church’s. From Christ “the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth… maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love” (Eph 4:16), and the man who lets go the Head is severed from the body “which by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God” (Col 2:19). Every joint supplies; the body grows by contact, not by a member’s private vigour.
webster_summary: The articulations at which bones and members are joined; in Scripture the seat of strength or of collapse, the finest seam the word of God divides, and the figure of the church’s knitting to its Head.
webster_full: JOINT, n. The joining of two or more things; the place where two bodies or parts of a body are united.
Old French joint, from Latin jungere, to join.
In anatomy, an articulation; the seat of motion and of the body’s coherence.
Greek harmos, a fitting (Heb 4:12); haphe, a joint or point of contact by which supply passes (Eph 4:16; Col 2:19).
To be out of joint, or to have the joints loosed, is to lose all strength (Dan 5:6).
scriptures: Dan 5:6
Then the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Eph 4:16

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
Col 2:19
And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.
corruption_summary: The organic body of Eph 4:16 has been traded for a religion of spectators — Christianity without membership, without covenanted joints, without any obligation that a believer might actually be missed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a church without joints. It is now ordinary for people who profess Christ to hold no membership anywhere, to attend by preference and at a distance, and to describe this as faith unencumbered by institutions; the broadcast sermon replaces the assembly, the podcast replaces the elder, and no covenanted body knows whether the man is walking in the truth or has quietly stopped. Eph 4:16 does not permit the arrangement. The growth of the body comes by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part. A joint is a point of contact through which supply passes; a member joined to no one supplies nothing and receives nothing, whatever his opinions about the church universal. Col 2:19 states the danger at its worst: the one who does not hold the Head is cut off from the nourishment ministered by joints and bands. The New Testament knows no Christianity that is not embodied in a local congregation, under elders, at a table, with discipline — a joint fastened to other joints.

Recover the doctrine of union, in its two inseparable directions. First, union with Christ the Head: the body has no life, no supply, and no growth except from Him, and the increase it experiences is the increase of God, not the yield of programmes. Second, union with the members: joined together and compacted, which the Puritans understood as covenant membership with real obligations, real submission, and real love. Then let the other two uses of the joint do their work. Heb 4:12 keeps the assembly honest — the word divides the joints and marrow, and it discerns thoughts and intents, so no man sits under preaching merely as an observer; he is being opened. And Dan 5:6 keeps the confident sober. Belshazzar had a kingdom, a feast, and the vessels of the house of God on his table, and one line of divine handwriting loosed the joints of his loins. Strength held together by anything but Christ comes apart at the joints on the day it is tested.
roots_summary: The articulations that hold a frame together; in Scripture loosed in terror, divided by the word, and knit into one body under its Head.
roots_lines: Joints — Latin jungere, to join, through Old French joint.
Greek harmos, a fitting (Heb 4:12); haphe, a contact through which supply passes.
Dan 5:6 — the joints of the loins loosed: strength undone by a written sentence.
Heb 4:12 — the word divides joints and marrow, the finest seam in a man.
Eph 4:16 and Col 2:19 — the church grows by supply passing through every joint.
usage: Every joint supplieth: the body grows by contact, not by private vigour.
Col 2:19 warns that not holding the Head cuts a man off from all nourishment.
Belshazzar’s loosed joints show what a kingdom’s strength is worth under judgment.

etymology: From the Old Norse skalli, a bald head, or the Saxon scelle, a shell; rendering the Hebrew gulgoleth (whence Golgotha) and the Greek kranion, the bony case of the head, translated Calvary in the Latin.
biblical_def: The skull is the bone that houses the brain and outlasts the flesh, and Scripture brings it forward at moments of judgment. Abimelech, having murdered seventy brethren on one stone and burned a tower full of men and women, laid siege to Thebez, and “a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech’s head, and all to brake his skull” (Jdg 9:53); the usurper who feared nothing so much as dying by a woman’s hand died by one, and asked his armourbearer to hide it, which the Holy Ghost declined to do. Of Jezebel they found “no more of her than the skull, and the feet, and the palms of her hands” (2Ki 9:35), the word of the LORD by Elijah fulfilled to the letter. But the word reaches its height at a bare rise outside Jerusalem: “a place called Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull” (Mat 27:33), where He bearing His cross went forth (Joh 19:17). The name is not incidental. At the place of the skull, the head of the serpent was bruised, as was promised in Eden to the seed of the woman — and the bruising cost the Heel everything. There, where death displayed its emblem, death was defeated; and the crushed skull of the tyrant in Judges and the emptied skull of Jezebel become dark rehearsals for the one head that was crushed at Calvary, and the one Head that rose.
webster_summary: The bony case of the head; in Scripture broken in judgment upon tyrants, and the name of the place outside Jerusalem where Christ was crucified.
webster_full: SKULL, n. The bone which forms the exterior of the head, and incloses the brain; the cranium.
Old Norse skalli, a bald head; compare Saxon scelle, a shell or case.
Hebrew gulgoleth, a skull or head, used also for a poll or head-count (Num 1:2).
From gulgoleth comes Golgotha; the Greek kranion; the Latin calvaria, whence Calvary.
Broken in judgment (Jdg 9:53); the name of the place of the crucifixion (Mat 27:33; Mar 15:22; Joh 19:17).
scriptures: Jdg 9:53
And a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull.
And they went to bury her: but they found no more of her than the skull, and the feet, and the palms of her hands.
And when they were come unto a place called Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull,
And he bearing his cross went forth into a place called the place of a skull, which is called in the Hebrew Golgotha:
corruption_summary: The place of a skull is sanitised into a symbol of solidarity or sacrificial love in general, and penal substitution — the wrath actually borne there — is slandered as divine cruelty.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the emptying of Golgotha. Progressive evangelicalism has for a generation taught that a Father punishing a Son is a monstrous doctrine — Steve Chalke’s notorious charge of “cosmic child abuse” is the best-known formula — and has offered instead a cross that reveals God’s solidarity with sufferers, exposes the violence of empire, or demonstrates love without satisfying justice. The place of a skull is thereby made a place of pathos and nothing more. Scripture will not have it. He was wounded for our transgressions; it pleased the LORD to bruise Him; He was made sin for us, made a curse for us, His soul an offering for sin, and He bore the wrath that was ours by right. Take substitution away and the name of the hill becomes unintelligible: there is no reason for a Sinless Man to die at a skull-shaped place of execution unless He is dying in the room and stead of the guilty. And the objection collapses on the doctrine of the Trinity, for the Son is not a third party conscripted by an angry Father; He is God the Son laying down His life of Himself, no man taking it from Him, the Father and the Son of one will in the salvation of the elect.

Recover the name and let it preach. Golgotha means the skull, and the skull is death’s own emblem — the last thing left of Jezebel, the thing broken in Abimelech, the bone that grins after the flesh is gone. God chose that hill and that name for the death of His Son, and there fulfilled the first promise ever made to fallen man: the seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent’s head, and thou shalt bruise his heel (Gen 3:15). The head-wound is mortal and the heel-wound is not, though the heel-wound was agony and blood. So the sequence in Judges is a shadow rather than a coincidence: a woman’s hand, a stone, a tyrant’s crushed skull, and a city delivered. At Calvary the seed of the woman took the stone Himself, and the tyrant whose head was broken was the old serpent. That is why the church has never been able to keep the cross as a symbol of tragedy. It is a place of execution turned into the trophy of a conquest, and the empty tomb three days later is the receipt.
roots_summary: The bony case of the head; Hebrew gulgoleth, whence Golgotha — the place outside the city where the serpent’s head was bruised.
roots_lines: Skull — Old Norse skalli, a bald head; the cranium or bony case.
Hebrew gulgoleth, skull, also used of a head-count or poll (Num 1:2).
Gulgoleth → Golgotha; Greek kranion; Latin calvaria → Calvary.
Jdg 9:53 and 2Ki 9:35 — broken and bared skulls as executed judgment.
Gen 3:15 supplies the key: the head bruised, the heel bruised, at the place of a skull.
usage: Golgotha is simply the Hebrew for skull; Calvary is the Latin of the same word.
Abimelech’s crushed skull and Jezebel’s bare one are judgments fulfilled to the letter.
Read Gen 3:15 at Mat 27:33 — head and heel, at the place of a skull.

etymology: From the Saxon bridel, a rein or curb, akin to bregdan, to draw or braid; rendering the Hebrew resen and metheg, the headstall and bit of a beast, and the Greek chalinos, the bit, whence the verb chalinagogeo, to lead by the bit, to bridle.
biblical_def: A bridle is the headgear by which a rider governs a beast that will not govern itself, and Scripture makes it the standing figure for restraint — imposed from without upon the brute, chosen from within by the wise. The rebuke is plain: “Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle” (Psa 32:9). The verse stands in the psalm of forgiveness, immediately after the promise “I will guide thee with mine eye,” and that is the whole argument: a son is led by a look, a mule by iron in the mouth. To be handled by force is not a compliment; God will govern His people either way, and the choice belongs to them. David takes up the same figure for his own tongue: “I will keep my mouth with a bridle, while the wicked is before me” (Psa 39:1) — deliberate, prayed-for restraint at exactly the moment when speech would be easiest and worst. James makes it the test of a man’s religion: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man’s religion is vain” (Jas 1:26), and then presses the figure to its conclusion — he that offends not in word is able also to bridle the whole body (Jas 3:2), for a bit in a horse’s mouth turns the whole animal. Govern the tongue and you have hold of the man.
webster_summary: The headstall, bit, and reins by which a horse is governed; hence a curb, a restraint, and the biblical figure for governing the tongue and thereby the whole man.
webster_full: BRIDLE, n. The instrument with which a horse is governed and restrained by a rider, consisting of a headstall, a bit, and reins.
Saxon bridel, akin to bregdan, to draw, braid, or restrain.
A restraint; a curb; a check. To bridle, to restrain, guide, or govern.
Hebrew resen, a halter or bridle; metheg, a bit (Psa 32:9).
Greek chalinos, a bit (Jas 3:3); chalinagogeo, to bridle or lead by the bit (Jas 1:26).
scriptures: Psa 32:9
Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee.
Psa 39:1
To the chief Musician, even to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David. I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a bridle, while the wicked is before me.
Jas 1:26
If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain.
Jas 3:2
For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.
corruption_summary: Restraint itself is now suspect: authenticity is preached as the highest virtue, unfiltered speech as honesty, and self-government as repression — the exact inversion of Jas 1:26.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is expressive individualism, which teaches that the self is discovered by being expressed and that any curb upon expression is a falsification of the person. In that scheme “speak your truth” is a moral duty, the unfiltered comment is prized as honesty, and the man who holds his tongue is charged with suppressing himself. Scripture inverts the entire evaluation. The unbridled tongue is not the authentic man liberated; it is the mule, the beast without understanding, requiring iron because it will not take a look (Psa 32:9). And the deception runs inward before it runs outward: he that bridleth not his tongue deceiveth his own heart, and his religion is vain (Jas 1:26) — a man may hold sound doctrine, attend faithfully, and be undone by his mouth. The digital age has removed nearly every friction that once slowed speech, so that a man may now publish his worst half-second to thousands, and it has attached applause to the sharpest tongue. Nothing about the mechanism changes the diagnosis; it only widens the ruin, since the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity, set on fire of hell.

Recover the doctrine that self-government is a fruit of the Spirit, not a repression of the self. Temperance stands last in the list of Gal 5:22–23 and belongs to the same Spirit who gives love and joy; the bridled tongue is evidence of grace, not of a cramped nature. Note carefully that no man bridles himself into salvation: James says the tongue can no man tame, and the taming that does occur comes from the new heart out of whose abundance the mouth speaks. But note equally that the bridled man gains, rather than loses, mastery — a bit in a horse’s mouth turns the whole body (Jas 3:3), and he that offends not in word is able to bridle the whole body (Jas 3:2). Government of the tongue is therefore the handle by which a whole life is steered, which is why David set a bridle on his mouth precisely while the wicked were before him (Psa 39:1), when silence would be misread as weakness. And Psa 32:9 leaves the sweetest motive: God would rather guide His children with His eye. The believer who learns to be led by a look is spared the bit.
roots_summary: The bit and reins by which a beast is governed; Scripture’s figure for restraint of the tongue, and thereby of the whole man.
roots_lines: Bridle — Saxon bridel, from bregdan, to draw or restrain.
Hebrew resen, halter; metheg, bit (Psa 32:9).
Greek chalinos, a bit; chalinagogeo, to lead by the bit (Jas 1:26; 3:2).
Psa 32:9 follows “I will guide thee with mine eye” — a son by a look, a mule by iron.
Jas 3:3 — the bit turns the whole horse; the tongue governed governs the man.
usage: Psa 32:9 is a rebuke, not a method: God prefers to guide His children with His eye.
An unbridled tongue makes a man’s religion vain, however sound his doctrine (Jas 1:26).
David bridled his mouth while the wicked were before him — restraint at the hardest hour.
